parts.problem_md:
A school has 40 staff and 490 students. Before this year's summer festival, the headteacher wants to survey a sample of the staff and students about their opinions of the festival.

The headteacher first suggests asking the staff and students who are helping to run the festival.

Give a reason why this method is unsatisfactory.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The people helping to run the festival are likely to be more enthusiastic about it than other staff and students, so their opinions may not represent everyone's**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A reason in context, e.g. helpers are likely to have more positive opinions of the festival; staff and students who are not helping have no chance of being chosen; or helpers may have discussed the festival together, so their opinions are not independent. "Biased" or "not representative" without a reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
Instead, the headteacher numbers all 530 staff and students from 1 to 530 and uses a calculator to generate random digits. The first 20 random digits are as follows.

1 2 7 3 9 4 0 6 5 1 2 7 8 8 3 4 8 8 2 0

The numbers of the first two people in the sample are 127 and 394.

Use these digits to find the numbers of the next two people in the sample.
parts.solution_md:
The people are numbered up to 530, so read the digits in blocks of three

*127, 394, 065, 127, 883, 488*

Take the blocks after 394 in turn, ignoring any number already chosen and any number greater than 530

*065 gives person 65*

*127 has already been chosen, so ignore it*

*883 is greater than 530, so ignore it*

*488 gives person 488*

**Final answer:** **65 and 488**

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 65 (accept 065).
> 
> **B1**: 488, with only two numbers given in total.
> 
> Numbers that should have been ignored (127 or 883) listed in the answer lose the second mark.

parts.problem_md:
A fast-food chain is planning to introduce a new vegan menu, and a researcher is employed to investigate customers' opinions before it is launched.

At 2 pm on a Wednesday, the researcher gives each customer eating in one branch of the chain a different number. The researcher then uses a random number generator to choose half of these customers to survey, ignoring any numbers that do not correspond to a customer.

Explain why this method produces a random sample of the customers in the branch at that time.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Every customer in the branch has a number, so each customer has an equal chance of being chosen**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Every customer (in the branch at that time) has an equal chance of being selected. "Because random numbers are used" or "because it is chosen at random" without reference to an equal chance does not score.

parts.problem_md: Give a reason why the opinions of the customers in this sample may not be representative of the opinions of all the chain's customers.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The sample only includes customers eating at one branch at 2 pm on a Wednesday, and people who eat at other times, on other days or at other branches may have different opinions**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A reason in context, e.g. only one time of day or one day of the week is used (people at work or school are missed); only one branch is used, which may not reflect other areas; or only people already eating fast food are asked, not potential vegan customers. "Biased" or "not representative" without a reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
A beauty company, Glow & Behold, releases an advertisement for its new product, 'Face Amazifier'. The small print at the bottom of the advertisement says:

'56% of 25 existing customers agree that the product makes your face feel more amazing.'

Some people complain that the advertisement is misleading.

Explain why the choice of sample may lead to bias.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Existing customers already buy from the company, so they are more likely to have a favourable opinion of its products than people who use other brands**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A reason in context, e.g. existing customers are likely to like the company's products already, or people who do not buy from the company have no chance of being asked. "It is biased" or "it is not representative" without a reason does not score.

parts.problem_md: Give a different reason why the figure in the advertisement may not be reliable.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The sample of 25 is very small compared with the number of people who might buy the product**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The sample is small (only 25 people). A repeat of the reason given in part (a), or "not random" with no explanation, does not score.

parts.problem_md:
Computer components produced by an electronics company are each given a unique serial number. A34X processing chips are produced in batches of 2500. For quality control, the company tests a random sample of 20 A34X chips from each batch.

The company will use four-digit random numbers in order to select the 20 A34X chips from each batch.

Briefly explain why the chips in a batch must first be numbered, for example from 0001 to 2500, before the four-digit random numbers are used.
parts.solution_md:
Each random number must match exactly one chip in the batch

**Final answer:** **The serial numbers are unique across everything the company makes, so in a batch they do not run from 0001 to 2500 and a four-digit random number would not match a chip in the batch**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A reason referring to the serial numbers, e.g. they are not the numbers 0001 to 2500, they may have more than four digits, or they are not consecutive, so a random number would not correspond to a chip in this batch. Accept "so that every chip in the batch has a number that a four-digit random number can select".

parts.problem_md: Explain how the company can use four-digit random numbers in order to sample the A34X chips.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Number the chips in the batch from 0001 to 2500, then generate four-digit random numbers**

**Final answer:** **Select the chip whose number matches each random number generated**

**Final answer:** **Ignore 0000, any number greater than 2500 and any number that has already been used**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Continue until 20 different chips have been selected**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Selecting the chips that match the random numbers, with numbers that do not correspond to a chip (0000 or greater than 2500) ignored.
> 
> **B1**: Repeated numbers ignored and the process continued until 20 different chips are chosen.
> 
> Alternative method: allocating four numbers to each chip (e.g. 0000 to 0003 for the first chip, 0004 to 0007 for the second, and so on) so that no random number is wasted scores the first mark; the second mark still needs repeats of the same chip ignored until 20 different chips are chosen.

parts.problem_md:
For each scenario below, state, giving a reason, whether it could lead to bias in the data collected.

(i) In a survey of adults' health, a sample of people aged 70 or over is used.

(ii) To find out how much time students spend on homework each week, a teacher asks the students who attend the after-school homework club.

(iii) Randomly sampling 20 people from a population of 100 by assigning each person in the population a unique two-digit number (00-99) and then selecting 20 using a two-digit random number generator.
parts.solution_md:
A sample is biased if some members of the population are more likely to be chosen than others, so that the sample does not represent the population

(i)

**Final answer:** **Yes, because people aged 70 or over are more likely to be in poorer health than younger adults, so the sample does not represent all adults**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **Yes, because students who go to a homework club are likely to spend more time on homework than other students**

**[B1]**

(iii)

**Final answer:** **No, because each person has their own number from 00 to 99, so every person has an equal chance of being selected**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Could lead to bias, with a reason in context, e.g. older people tend to have poorer health, or younger adults are excluded from a survey of all adults.
> 
> **B1**: Could lead to bias, with a reason in context, e.g. students at the homework club are likely to do more homework than average, or students who do not attend have no chance of being chosen.
> 
> **B1**: Would not lead to bias, because every person has an equal chance of being selected (the numbers 00 to 99 match the 100 people exactly).
> 
> Each mark needs both the decision and a reason. "Biased", "not random" or "not representative" on its own does not score.

parts.problem_md:
A flatpack furniture company, Flat & Fabulous, has a testing facility where its products are put through a series of safety and quality checks.

Give two reasons why it is necessary for the company to use a sample rather than testing every item it produces.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The company produces a very large number of items, so testing every one would take too long**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Safety testing may damage or destroy the items, so tested items might not be able to be sold**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: One valid reason, e.g. too time-consuming, too costly, or too many items produced.
> 
> **B1**: A second, different valid reason, e.g. items may be damaged or destroyed by testing, so could not be sold.
> 
> Two versions of the same idea (e.g. "it takes too long" and "it is too slow") score only one mark. Vague answers such as "it is inconvenient" do not score.

parts.problem_md:
An online magazine offers both free content and paid-for content, and has a large number of readers. Before making any changes, the editor decides to carry out a sample survey to obtain the opinions of the readers.

(i) State one advantage of carrying out a sample survey rather than surveying all the readers.

(ii) The editor finds the mean age, $\overline{x}$ years, of the readers in a sample. Explain briefly why $\overline{x}$ is only an estimate of the mean age, $μ$ years, of all the magazine's readers.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

**Final answer:** **A sample survey is quicker and cheaper than surveying every reader**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **The sample contains only some of the readers, and a different sample would give a different value of **$\overline{x}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A valid advantage, e.g. less time, less cost, or less data to process. "It is easier" alone does not score.
> 
> **B1**: Only part of the population is included, or the sample mean varies from sample to sample. Practical reasons such as readers giving the wrong age do not score.

parts.problem_md:
The editor decides to gather opinions from only the 3750 readers who pay for the additional content. A random sample of 25 of these readers is chosen.

Give a reason why this sample may not be representative of all the magazine's readers.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Readers who use only the free content have no chance of being chosen, and they may have different opinions from readers who pay**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A reason in context, e.g. readers of only the free content are excluded, or paying readers may have different views from other readers. "The sample is too small" does not score here, and "biased" or "not representative" without a reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
A charity runs four sloth sanctuaries, which care for 24, 40, 16 and 56 sloths. The charity chooses a sample of sloths from each sanctuary for health tests.

At the sanctuary with 40 sloths, the sloths are numbered 1 to 40. The charity generates random three-digit numbers and allocates them to the sloths as follows.

000 to 024 to sloth 1, 025 to 049 to sloth 2, and so on, up to 975 to 999 to sloth 40

The first four random numbers generated are 137, 862, 140 and 503.

(i) Find the numbers of the first three sloths in the sample.

(ii) Explain why this method is more efficient than giving each sloth a single three-digit number.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

Each sloth has 25 numbers, so sloth $n$ has the numbers from $25 ( n - 1 )$ to $25 n - 1$

*137 is in 125 to 149, so it gives sloth 6*

*862 is in 850 to 874, so it gives sloth 35*

*140 is in 125 to 149, which is sloth 6 again, so ignore it*

*503 is in 500 to 524, so it gives sloth 21*

**Final answer:** **6, 35 and 21**

**[B1 B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **Every three-digit random number corresponds to a sloth, so no numbers are wasted**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Sloths 6 and 35.
> 
> **B1**: Sloth 21, with the repeat (140, sloth 6) ignored and only three sloths given.
> 
> **B1**: No random numbers are wasted (with single numbers, 960 of the 1000 numbers would have to be ignored). Accept "fewer numbers need to be generated". "It is more random" or "it is fairer" does not score.

parts.problem_md:
The charity tests 3, 5, 2 and 7 sloths from the sanctuaries with 24, 40, 16 and 56 sloths respectively. The sloths tested at the sanctuary with 16 sloths weighed less, on average, than those tested at the other three sanctuaries.

Give a reason why this does not necessarily mean that the sloths at the sanctuary with 16 sloths are less healthy than those at the other sanctuaries.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Only 2 sloths were tested at that sanctuary, which is too small a sample to be reliable; they may simply have been smaller than average**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A valid reason, e.g. the sample of 2 sloths is very small; the two sloths may happen to be younger or smaller; or a lower weight does not necessarily mean poorer health. "Biased" or "not representative" without a reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
A sloth can be released into the wild once it has reached the age of 3 and has a healthy weight.

Explain why the results of these tests are of little use for deciding which sloths are ready to be released into the wild.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The decision needs the age and weight of each individual sloth, but most of the sloths were not tested**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Information about every individual sloth is needed, and a sample only gives information about the sloths tested (most sloths were not tested). Accept "the sample only describes the sanctuary as a whole, not each sloth".

parts.problem_md:
A factory produces paper fruit baskets. The breaking load of a basket is the maximum load that it can carry before its handles break. A farm buys 15 000 of these baskets and wishes to test some of them to investigate their breaking load.

Give two reasons why it is necessary to test a sample rather than all 15 000 baskets.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Testing a basket's breaking load destroys it, so testing every basket would leave none for the farm to use**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **There are 15 000 baskets, so testing them all would take too long and cost too much**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Testing is destructive: tested baskets are broken and cannot be used.
> 
> **B1**: A second, different reason, e.g. testing 15 000 baskets would take too long, be too costly, or the population is too large.
> 
> Two versions of the same point score one mark.

parts.problem_md:
The farm tests a random sample of 6 baskets. The breaking loads, in kg, are as follows.

2.035 1.975 2.128 1.898 2.112 1.999

(i) Without carrying out any calculations, comment on the factory's claim that the mean breaking load of the baskets is 2 kg.

(ii) Give one criticism of the sample used by the farm.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

Compare each load with 2 kg

**Final answer:** **The claim seems reasonable, because the breaking loads are all close to 2 kg, with three above and three below**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **A sample of only 6 baskets out of 15 000 is too small to give a reliable result**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The claim appears reasonable, with a reason from the data (values close to 2 kg, or three above and three below). The comment must not be definite: "the claim is correct" does not score. Accept "true on average, but half the baskets break below 2 kg, so the claim is misleading for individual baskets".
> 
> **B1**: The sample is too small (only 6 baskets). "Not representative" alone does not score, since the sample is random.

parts.problem_md:
A researcher wishes to measure the heights of a random sample of the 2400 giraffes in a large nature reserve. Each giraffe has a unique four-digit identification number from 0001 to 2400.

The researcher decides to select the giraffes with identification numbers 0001 to 0100.

(i) Explain why this method of selection will not produce a random sample.

(ii) Describe how the researcher could use random numbers to select a random sample of 100 giraffes.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

**Final answer:** **Giraffes numbered 0101 to 2400 have no chance of being selected, so not every giraffe has an equal chance**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **Generate four-digit random numbers and select the giraffe with each number**

**Final answer:** **Ignore 0000 and any number greater than 2400**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Ignore any number already chosen, and continue until 100 different giraffes have been selected**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Giraffes numbered above 0100 have no chance of being chosen (not every giraffe has an equal chance). Accept "the numbers may have been given out in a pattern, e.g. by age or arrival date". "Not random" or "biased" without a reason does not score.
> 
> **B1**: Four-digit random numbers used, with 0000 and numbers greater than 2400 ignored.
> 
> **B1**: Repeated numbers ignored, continuing until 100 different giraffes are chosen.

parts.problem_md:
The researcher measures the heights of the 100 giraffes in the sample and finds their mean height, $\overline{h}$ m.

Explain why $\overline{h}$ is only an estimate of the mean height, $μ$ m, of all the giraffes in the reserve.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Only 100 of the 2400 giraffes were measured, and a different random sample would give a different value of **$\overline{h}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Only a sample (not the whole population) was measured, or the sample mean varies from sample to sample. Measurement errors (e.g. giraffes being hard to measure) do not score.

parts.problem_md:
The owner of a revision website, Cram Central, wants to find out what users would like to see on the website in future. The website has over 650 000 users, and about 15% of them have signed up to its mailing list to get updates.

An employee suggests emailing a questionnaire to everyone on the mailing list and using the replies.

Give two reasons why the users who reply would not form a random sample of the website's users.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Only users on the mailing list can be chosen, so the 85% of users who have not signed up have no chance of being included**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **The users who reply choose themselves, so they may be the keenest users and not typical of users in general**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Users not on the mailing list (about 85%) have no chance of being chosen.
> 
> **B1**: The replies are self-selected: only users who choose to reply are included, and they may differ from those who do not.
> 
> "Biased" or "not random" without a reason does not score. "The sample is too small" does not score.

parts.problem_md:
The owner decides instead to choose a random sample from the 4581 mailing-list subscribers who study one particular course. The subscribers are numbered from 1 to 4581 and the following random digits are used.

02743 45290 19027 44600 13880 00045 11279

The numbers of the first two subscribers in the sample are 274 and 3452.

Use the random digits to find the numbers of the next two subscribers in the sample.
parts.solution_md:
The subscribers are numbered up to 4581, so read the digits in blocks of four, ignoring the spaces

*0274, 3452, 9019, 0274, 4600, 1388, 0000, 4511*

Take the blocks after 3452 in turn, ignoring 0000, any number greater than 4581 and any number already chosen

*9019 is greater than 4581, so ignore it*

*0274 has already been chosen, so ignore it*

*4600 is greater than 4581, so ignore it*

*1388 gives subscriber 1388*

*0000 does not correspond to a subscriber, so ignore it*

*4511 gives subscriber 4511*

**Final answer:** **1388 and 4511**

**[B1 B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The spaces in a list of random digits are only there to make it easier to read. Read the digits as one continuous string, so a block of four can run across a space.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 1388.
> 
> **B1**: 4511, with only two numbers given in total.
> 
> Numbers that should have been ignored (9019, 274, 4600 or 0) listed in the answer lose the second mark.

parts.problem_md:
Stephan is researching the effects a new energy drink has on the glucose levels of students aged 13 to 18. He plans to measure the blood glucose levels of a random sample of 50 students.

Stephan uses an alphabetical list of 100 male students in his year group at the Sixth Form college he attends. All 100 have agreed to have a blood glucose test if they are selected.

Explain how Stephan could use a two-digit random number generator to choose a random sample of 50 students from his list.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Number the students on the list from 00 to 99 and generate two-digit random numbers, selecting the student with each number**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Ignore any number that has already been chosen, and continue until 50 different students have been selected**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Each of the 100 students given a different number (e.g. 00 to 99, or 01 to 100 with 00 standing for 100) and the students matching the random numbers selected.
> 
> **B1**: Repeated numbers ignored, continuing until 50 different students are chosen.

parts.problem_md: Explain how the data could be biased.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The list only includes male students, but Stephan is investigating students in general, so female students have no chance of being chosen**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A reason in context, e.g. only male students can be chosen, although the research is about all students aged 13 to 18; only students who volunteered (agreed to a blood test) can be chosen; only one year group (not ages 13 to 18) is included; or only one college is used. "Biased" or "not representative" without a reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
Freda wishes to investigate the flavour of ice cream preferred by people living in her town. She stands in a busy high street on a Sunday afternoon and asks shoppers to answer her questions.

Give two reasons why this method of selecting a sample is unsatisfactory.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Only people in that high street can be chosen, so people who shop elsewhere or stay at home have no chance of being selected**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Only people out on a Sunday afternoon can be chosen, so people who are working or busy at that time are missed**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A reason in context, e.g. only people on that high street can be chosen.
> 
> **B1**: A second, different reason, e.g. only people there on a Sunday afternoon; some groups (e.g. families out shopping) may be over-represented; shoppers may include visitors who do not live in the town.
> 
> "Biased", "not random" or "not representative" without a reason does not score. Two versions of the same point score one mark.

parts.problem_md:
Freda instead decides to choose a random sample of people from the electoral register for her town, which is a list of the adults who are registered to vote.

Give a reason why this sample may still not be representative of the people in her town who eat ice cream.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Children are not on the electoral register, so they have no chance of being chosen, even though many children eat ice cream**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Under-18s (children) are excluded from the register, or adults who are not registered to vote are excluded. The answer must link to who is missing from the list. "Not everyone votes" alone does not score.

parts.problem_md:
Freda posts a questionnaire to each person in her sample and uses only the replies that she receives.

Explain why the people who reply may not form a random sample.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The people who reply choose themselves, and they may be those with stronger views about ice cream or more free time, so they may differ from those who do not reply**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The people who reply are self-selected, so they may differ from those who do not reply (e.g. stronger opinions, more interest in ice cream, more free time). "Not everyone will reply" alone does not score.

parts.problem_md:
A company wants to survey 15% of its staff to find out whether employees would like to work from home on some days each week. The company has 580 members of staff.

Describe how the company can randomly sample its staff.
parts.solution_md:
Find the size of the sample first

$0 . 15 \times 580 = 87$

**Final answer:** **Make a list of all 580 members of staff and number them from 001 to 580**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Generate three-digit random numbers, ignoring 000, any number greater than 580 and any number already chosen**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Continue until 87 different members of staff have been selected**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A list of all the staff, each given a different number (e.g. 001 to 580, or 1 to 580).
> 
> **B1**: Random numbers used to select staff, with numbers that do not correspond to a member of staff and repeated numbers ignored.
> 
> **B1**: Selection continued until 87 members of staff are chosen. Accept "15% of the staff" if 87 is not stated.

parts.problem_md:
Clyde works at an orangutan sanctuary and part of his job involves measuring the weight of each of its orangutans once a week.

The weights, to the nearest kg, of all their 20 adult males are listed below:

52, 57, 63, 80, 56, 66, 101, 68, 55, 96, 70, 62, 66, 64, 99, 91, 55, 92, 73, 61

State two reasons why, in this case, it is important that Clyde weighs every orangutan rather than taking a sample of them.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The weights are used to monitor the health of each individual orangutan, so every orangutan needs to be weighed**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **There are only 20 orangutans, so weighing them all is quick and practical**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A reason linked to the purpose, e.g. the sanctuary needs to know the weight (health) of each individual orangutan, not just an average.
> 
> **B1**: The population is small (only 20), so weighing every orangutan is feasible.

parts.problem_md:
The sanctuary decides to trial a new medication by testing it on 5 of their 20 adult male orangutans. Clyde assigns each orangutan one unique 2-digit number (from 00 to 99), then uses a 2-digit random number generator to select which orangutans will be given the new medication. Clyde ignores any numbers generated that are not assigned to an orangutan.

(i) Explain how Clyde's system of selecting orangutans will produce a random sample of the population.

(ii) Explain how Clyde could make more efficient use of the 2-digit random number generator.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

**Final answer:** **Every orangutan has its own number, so each orangutan has an equal chance of being selected**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **There are 100 two-digit numbers and 20 orangutans, so each orangutan can be given 5 numbers**

**Final answer:** **Give the first orangutan the numbers 00 to 04, the second 05 to 09, and so on, up to 95 to 99 for the twentieth**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Then every number generated corresponds to an orangutan, so no numbers are wasted**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Each orangutan has an equal (or non-zero) chance of being selected. "Because random numbers are used" alone does not score.
> 
> **B1**: Each orangutan given 5 numbers, e.g. 00 to 04, 05 to 09, …, 95 to 99. Any allocation of 5 different numbers to each orangutan is accepted.
> 
> **B1**: Every random number now corresponds to an orangutan, so none are ignored (numbers that select an orangutan already chosen are still ignored).

parts.problem_md:
A local council wants to find out the opinions of residents about opening a new care home. The council numbers the 726 adults living in one village from 1 to 726 and uses a calculator to generate random digits. The first 20 random digits are as follows.

3 1 8 0 7 2 9 5 0 3 1 8 7 0 4 6 1 5 2 9

The numbers of the first two adults in the sample are 318 and 72.

Write down the numbers of the next two adults in the sample.
parts.solution_md:
The adults are numbered up to 726, so read the digits in blocks of three

*318, 072, 950, 318, 704, 615*

Take the blocks after 072 in turn, ignoring any number greater than 726 and any number already chosen

*950 is greater than 726, so ignore it*

*318 has already been chosen, so ignore it*

*704 gives adult 704*

*615 gives adult 615*

**Final answer:** **704 and 615**

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 704.
> 
> **B1**: 615, with only two numbers given in total.
> 
> Numbers that should have been ignored (950 or 318) listed in the answer lose the second mark.

parts.problem_md:
To choose more adults, the council starts again from the second random digit, 1, and obtains the numbers 180 and 503.

Explain why this method will not produce a random sample.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The digits have already been used, so these numbers are not independent of the numbers already chosen**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The numbers are not independent of those already obtained, e.g. the same digits are being reused, the new numbers overlap the earlier ones, or only a finite list of digits is being used. "Not random" or "biased" without a reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
For each scenario below, state, giving a reason, whether the scenario could lead to bias in the data collected.

(i) To estimate the mean height of adults in a town, a researcher measures the heights of the members of the town's basketball club.

(ii) To find out how often people in a city use public transport, a council surveys people waiting at a bus stop.

(iii) A sample of 5 dogs from a population of 10 at a rescue home being randomly produced by assigning each dog a single digit number (from 0 to 9) and using a random number generator to select which dogs are selected for the sample.
parts.solution_md:
A sample is biased if some members of the population are more likely to be chosen than others, so that the sample does not represent the population

(i)

**Final answer:** **Yes, because basketball players are likely to be taller than adults in general**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **Yes, because people waiting at a bus stop are likely to use public transport more often than people in general**

**[B1]**

(iii)

**Final answer:** **No, because each dog has its own digit, so every dog has an equal chance of being selected**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Could lead to bias, with a reason in context, e.g. basketball players tend to be taller than average, or adults who are not in the club have no chance of being chosen.
> 
> **B1**: Could lead to bias, with a reason in context, e.g. people at a bus stop are more likely to use public transport, or people who never use buses have almost no chance of being chosen.
> 
> **B1**: Would not lead to bias, because every dog has an equal chance of being selected.
> 
> Each mark needs both the decision and a reason. "Biased", "not random" or "not representative" on its own does not score.

parts.problem_md:
The wingspans of a sample of 25 flamingos in a nature reserve were measured to the nearest centimetre.

(i) State one condition needed for the sample to be a random sample.

(ii) A researcher suggests that collecting the data on a weekday morning might cause the sample to be biased. State, with a reason, whether the researcher's suggestion is valid.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

**Final answer:** **Every flamingo in the reserve must have an equal chance of being selected**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **The suggestion is not valid, because a flamingo's wingspan does not depend on the day of the week or the time of day**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Every flamingo in the reserve has an equal chance of being chosen. Accept "the flamingos are chosen independently of each other". "It is chosen at random" alone does not score.
> 
> **B1**: Not valid, with a reason, e.g. wingspan is not affected by the day or time of measurement. Accept "valid" only with a reason linked to which flamingos can be caught or seen at that time (e.g. only flamingos near the feeding area in the morning can be measured). A decision with no reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
To check the quality of produce delivered to a restaurant, the head chef tastes one item from each box of produce as soon as it arrives. The chef opens each box in turn and tastes the item at the top of the box.

(i) Give a reason why it is necessary for the chef to test a sample rather than every item of produce.

(ii) Give a reason why the chef may not test every type of produce that is delivered.

(iii) Explain why the chef's method does not give a random sample of the produce.
parts.solution_md:
(i)

**Final answer:** **An item is eaten when it is tested, so if every item were tasted there would be nothing left to cook or sell**

**[B1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **Only one item is tasted from each box, so if a box contains several types of produce, some types are not tested**

**[B1]**

(iii)

**Final answer:** **Only the item at the top of each box can be chosen, so items lower in the box have no chance of being selected**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Testing destroys (uses up) the produce, or testing every item would take too long.
> 
> **B1**: Only one item per box is tasted, so a box containing more than one type of produce has some types untested.
> 
> **B1**: Items not at the top of a box have no chance (not an equal chance) of being chosen. "Biased" or "not random" without a reason does not score.

parts.problem_md:
The manager of a supermarket wants to find out how far shoppers travel to shop there.

Give a reason why a sample of shoppers should be used rather than the whole population of shoppers.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The supermarket has a very large number of shoppers, so asking every one of them would take too long**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A valid reason, e.g. the population is too large, it would be too time-consuming or too costly, or the population of shoppers keeps changing. "It is easier" alone does not score.

parts.problem_md:
One weekday lunchtime, an employee stands at the entrance of the supermarket and asks the first 10 shoppers who arrive how far they have travelled.

State two criticisms of this method of choosing a sample.
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **Only shoppers who arrive at lunchtime on a weekday can be chosen, and they may travel different distances from shoppers at other times, such as evenings or weekends**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **A sample of only 10 shoppers is too small to give a reliable result**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A criticism in context, e.g. only lunchtime (or weekday) shoppers can be selected; people who shop at other times may travel different distances (e.g. local workers at lunchtime).
> 
> **B1**: A second, different criticism, e.g. the sample of 10 is too small; only the first 10 shoppers can be chosen, so the others have no chance; shoppers arriving together are not independent; shoppers using another entrance cannot be chosen.
> 
> "Biased" or "not representative" without a reason does not score. Two versions of the same point score one mark.
